question: What is a token in the context of an LLM?
options: Exactly one word of English text
A sub-word chunk that is the atomic unit an LLM reads and writes
A single character of input
An API authentication key
explanation: Models process text as tokens, sub-word units. Common words are ~1 token but rare words, code, and punctuation split into several, so tokens are neither words nor characters.

question: Using the ~4-characters-per-token rule of thumb, roughly how many tokens is the string "agentic AI" (10 characters)?
options: ~1 token
~3 tokens
~10 tokens
~40 tokens
explanation: 10 characters / 4 is about 2 to 3 tokens. It is only an estimate since real tokenizers differ, but the key point is that tokens are far fewer than characters and not equal to words.

question: Which of these all draw from the same context-window budget in a single model call?
options: Only the conversation history
Only the input, never the generated output
The system prompt, tool schemas, conversation history, retrieved documents, and the reserved answer space
Only the tool schemas and the answer
explanation: The context window is one shared budget. System prompt, tool definitions, history, retrieved docs, and the room reserved for the answer all compete for it, which is why growing one shrinks another.

question: An agent's chat keeps growing and eventually the API call fails. What is the root cause?
options: The temperature was set too high
Total tokens (system + tools + history + answer) exceeded the context window
Too many tools were defined in the registry
The model got bored and refused
explanation: History accumulates every loop and shares the window with everything else. Once the total exceeds the window the call fails, which is exactly why you trim or summarize before calling.

question: A colleague argues: 'We picked a model with a huge context window, so we never have to manage context anymore.' Why is this reasoning flawed?
options: Bigger windows are actually smaller for input
Bigger windows cost more, run slower, and can dilute attention ('lost in the middle'), so good agents still curate context
Large windows silently truncate the system prompt first
Context windows do not affect cost at all
explanation: A larger window raises cost and latency and can degrade attention on middle content. Curating what goes into context still matters rather than dumping everything in.

question: Why is resending a large history on every agent loop iteration a problem?
options: It improves accuracy, so it is actually fine
It only matters when the agent processes images
Input tokens are re-billed each call and latency grows with tokens, so a big history across many loops is slow and expensive
It has no measurable cost or latency impact
explanation: You pay for input tokens on every call and latency scales with tokens generated and processed, so a large history multiplied across many loops is costly and slow, motivating compaction and caching.
